newsitem.title: USA: U.S West spot power firm, Calif. demand cited.
newsitem.headline: U.S West spot power firm, Calif. demand cited.

text.p: Spot power prices in the western U.S. were slightly firmer, with Northwest prices still being bid up by demand from water-logged northern California utilities, trade sources said Friday.
In addition, weather in the Pacific Northwest is getting colder, so utilities there "are reluctant to sell as much," said one California trader.
Flooding in central and northern California has led to curtailments at hydroelectric dams, which are being managed to minimize flooding while some have been damaged by the heavy flows.
The cutbacks are expected to last about a week, said industry sources.
"There isn't really a shortage of power, but the market came up to match Bonneville's prices," said one trader.
Bonneville Power Administration offered power for peak and off-peak hours through Monday, with high-end prices at $22.50 per megawatt hour (MWh) for non-firm peak power on Monday.
Traders cited lackluster market activity in the Southwest, where loads are seen capped by warm temperatures.
Firm, peak electricity at the California-Oregon border (COB) for Monday was quoted at $18.00-20.00 per megawatt hour (MWh), up from $14.00-16.00 early on Friday.
Off-peak COB for Monday was quoted at $11.00-12.00, up from $9.00-10.00 early on Friday.
Northwest prices rose in late trading on Friday when some buyers moved to cover near-term needs.
Monday firm, peak power at Mid-Columbia (Mid-C) was quoted at $18.00-$19.00, while off-peak was at $10.00-11.00.
Firm, peak Palo Verde (PV) electricity for Monday was quoted at $15.00-17.00, up from $13.00-15.00.
Off-peak PV for Monday was $8.00-9.00 per MWh.
Monday firm, peak prices at Four Corners were quoted at $15.00-17.00, with off-peak at $7.00-8.00.
